title: Can AI Help Gen Z Meaningfully Learn?
author: Research for Educators (reviewer); article reviewed by Sarah Chardonnens
summary: This piece reviews a 2025 systematic literature review by Sarah Chardonnens titled 'Adapting Educational Practices for Generation Z: Integrating Metacognitive Strategies and Artificial Intelligence,' examining what the research says about how Gen Z learns and whether AI can support or hinder that learning. Chardonnens identifies five themes: Gen Z's digitally-shaped cognitive patterns (non-linear, fragmented, platform-driven), the double-edged role of AI (adaptive feedback supports learning but heavy reliance decreases self-regulation), the attention and working memory costs of digital multitasking, intrinsic motivation patterns, and mental health implications of screen use. The reviewer notes that real teachers cannot and should not be replaced by AI, but that integrating AI feedback alongside teacher-led discussion can develop better self-regulation than either approach alone. Studies show students who frequently checked phones during learning performed 20% worse on memory retention tasks. Practical recommendations include formative assessment throughout the learning process rather than only at the end, active learning and project-based approaches, student-set learning goals with documented progress to build metacognition, and critical media literacy education. The article closes with an honest note of uncertainty: just as we are learning that screens in schools have not improved learning, we may learn the same about AI — the longitudinal data simply does not yet exist.
points: Heavy reliance on AI reduces students' ability to plan, monitor, and regulate their own learning — but AI feedback combined with teacher-led discussion actually develops stronger self-regulation and autonomy than either approach in isolation, which is the critical nuance for classroom integration decisions.

Gen Z's information-processing patterns are non-linear and fragmented: students prefer hyperlinked, modular structures over sequential lectures, a preference shaped by TikTok and Snapchat interaction patterns, which has real implications for how courses and units are designed.

Digital multitasking imposes measurable cognitive costs: students who frequently checked phones performed 20% worse on memory retention tasks than those who didn't, with the mechanism being impairment of working memory and knowledge integration rather than mere distraction.

Algorithmic bias is a live concern for AI in education: a platform trained on data limited to Western contexts may not be relevant or applicable in Latin American or South Asian educational settings, meaning AI personalization can inadvertently reinforce existing inequities.

The reviewer's closing question applies a healthy epistemic brake to AI enthusiasm: 'Just as we are learning that screens in school are actually not helping children learn better or more, will we learn the same about AI later?' — acknowledging that the absence of longitudinal data is itself a finding educators should not ignore.
quotes: Their cognitive, motivational, and behavioral patterns have been shaped by their immersion in the digital world. They are accustomed to fast, visual interactions from platforms like TikTok and Snapchat which meet their need for immediate connection. Gen Z-ers want to learn through personalized learning that offers real-time feedback.

The way Gen Z processes information is non-linear and often fragmented. Rather than learn about one topic in a straightforward, linear way, they prefer things like hyperlinks and modules. Think about a course or unit broken up into modules rather than a series of longer lectures.

Students who relied heavily on AI showed decreased ability to plan, monitor, and regulate their learning on their own. But when AI feedback was combined with teacher-led discussion, students developed better self-regulation and autonomy. TLDR: real teachers cannot and should not be replaced by AI, but teachers could integrate feedback and discussions about AI into their teaching.

Digital distractions also negatively impact working memory (undergrads who frequently checked their phones did 20% worse on memory retention than those who didn't). Digital distractions impede integration of knowledge and therefore cognition. Strategies such as pauses, reflective questions, and active engagement strategies supported information retention.

Take care to use AI to personalize learning without creating dependence. Students still need to develop the skills to learn independently. AI can be used for real time feedback in collaborative activities, potentially supporting social emotional development.

Just as we are learning that screens in school are actually not helping children learn better or more, will we learn the same about AI later? Regardless, we know for sure that Gen Z's learning behaviors have shifted, and those of us who teach them must also adapt to meet them where they are.
